commits.messageBody:
…md join tail

Review round on the Axis 2 raw STATE.md write guard:

- The write's own line is read up to the call's column, so
  `const p = path.join(dir, 'STATE.md'); fs.writeFileSync(p, c)` resolves.
  Statements are read last to first, a right-hand side ends at its own
  `;`, `p += x` is followed, and the next hop resumes before the followed statement, so a chain on
  one line resolves.
- Rule: that line (and a hop's cut line) is read only when it is plain
  statements. A line with `{`, `}`, `=>`, `function` or `for` is not read, and
  Axis 2 behaves on it exactly as before: telling a closure's enclosing
  variable from a shadowing parameter or block-scoped sibling needs a
  scope analysis, and four review passes found false positives in each
  approximation.
- A `path.join`/`path.resolve` (including `path.posix`/`path.win32`)
  whose last segment is a literal file name is decided by that literal,
  so a directory derived from statePath joined with 'ROADMAP.md' is no
  longer flagged (no allowlist could clear it, ADR-4629 Decision 5). A
  trailing comma is ignored; a '' or '.' tail names no file.
- Arrow functions and methods stay non-boundaries (stopping there would
  hide writes inside closures); the sibling-body cost is pinned as a
  `limit:` row.
- Template interpolations are extracted by brace depth; CRLF input
  resolves variable targets (`.` never matched the trailing `\r`).
- Tests: a row per finding and per review probe, `rule:` and `limit:`
  rows pinning the line rule, MAX-1 on the hop bound, and a fast-check
  property over names, filler, call shape, statePath-derived
  directories, and line endings.

commits.messageBody:
…r clears a raw STATE.md write

The raw-write axis took the nearest textual binding and ignored block and
arrow scope, so `const n = 'ROADMAP.md'` inside a closed `if` block or
arrow body cleared `fs.writeFileSync(path.join(d, n), c)` where `n` is a
parameter or an outer `const n = 'STATE.md'`.

Fail-safe minimum fix, not a scope tracker: a binding decides only when no
`{`, `}` or `=>` lies between the end of its right-hand side and the write
in the comment-stripped text. Past such a boundary, a const join tail no
longer clears (the whole-expression rule decides, as before the tail
pre-check), and the target chain keeps searching for an earlier binding of
the same name instead of stopping at the first one that misses STATE.md.
A binding that reaches STATE.md still reports at once, so closure writes
are unchanged. The rule only removes clears.

The const check is now anchored at the match start, so a later `const` in
the same statement span cannot mark a `let` as `const`.

New rows: the sibling-block probe (multi-line, one-line block, arrow
body), the outer-STATE/inner-ROADMAP shadow (directory from statePath and
from a plain parameter, and through the write target), controls for a
binding in the write's own body, a by-design row for the new fallback
(a const before a block that holds the write), and the whole-function
one-line probe as a known scope gap. Real tree: rawWriteViolations 0.

commits.messageBody:
…tay bounded

Every hop of resolvesToStatePath branched over each identifier of a
right-hand side, with no record of what it had already resolved. A file
with 60 `let vN = v0 + ... + v59;` lines, each followed by `{ }`, and
`fs.writeFileSync(v0 + ... + v59, c)` took 112 s to scan locally (20.4 s
in review 5558390402).

Each name's lookup is now memoized per write on (name, line, hops left),
in a context findRawStateWrites makes fresh per write, never in module
state. The verdict depends only on those and the scanned lines, so no
verdict moves: the old and new script agree on all 650 tracked files
that call fs.writeFileSync (964 findings, 0 differences). The 60-name
file now scans in about 1.1 s locally.

findRawStateWrites takes an optional stats object and reports
assignmentLookups, the nearestPrecedingAssignment calls it made (the
count is overwritten per call, not accumulated). A new row bounds that
count on the crafted shape at 20 names without a clock: 33215 calls
without the memo (the row fails), 1694 with it, against a bound of
2 * N * (N + 1) * MAX_TARGET_RESOLUTION_HOPS = 3360 (at
MAX_TARGET_RESOLUTION_HOPS = 4).

The bound is per write only. Residuals, measured locally:
- Cost scales with the number of writes, because the memo is rebuilt per
  write: the 60-name file with the write line repeated 40 times took
  48.6 s (634960 lookups).
- The assignment regex prefix backtracks on a long whitespace run: one
  40000-space line holding the name, plus one write, took 0.9 s (80000
  spaces: 3.1 s); with 20 writes, 17.6 s. origin/next's Axis 2 took 2 to
  8 ms on the same inputs.
commits.messageHeadline: ci(#5104): memoize raw-write target resolution so lookups per write s…

commits.messageBody:
…hared across a file's writes

A line holding a variable's name and a long whitespace run stalled the
raw-write scan, and the cost of a file grew with its number of writes.
One `const p<40000 spaces>x;` line followed by 20 writes took 10.8 s
locally, 22.6 s in review.

- The assignment regex matched `(?:^|[^.\w$])(?:const|let|var)?\s*NAME`,
  so every position of a whitespace run could start a match and
  backtrack over the rest of the run. Each match now starts at the name
  and a lookbehind reads the text before it; the language and the
  captured right-hand side are unchanged, and Axis 3 reads through the
  same regex. The typed form `[^=;]+?\s*=` is written `[^=;]+=` (same
  language). The for...of binding regex had the same overlap
  (`\s+(.+?)\s+of\b`); it now reads `(.*?\S)\s+of\b` after taking the
  keyword's whitespace whole, which reads the same pattern.
- nearestPrecedingAssignment takes an opt-in `cache`, one per file for
  Axis 2: each line is read at most once per name across every write,
  and the write's own line, cut at the call, is read per write
  (`firstLine`, never cached).
- A name's verdict below a write's line depends on the write only
  through whether a body boundary lies after that line, so those
  verdicts are shared by every write in the file, keyed on that flag.
  The boundary rule reads a per-file count of boundary lines instead of
  joining the lines between per write.
- findRawStateWrites no longer throws on a null `stats`, and reports
  `linesRead` beside `assignmentLookups`.

Probe, before -> after (local, ms): the whitespace line with N = 1, 5,
20 writes: 508, 2590, 10791 -> 5, 3, 6. Same with a type annotation:
1023 -> 4 (N = 1); with a for...of header: 985 -> 4 (N = 1); the
for...of header with the run also after its keyword did not finish in
300 s before, 5 ms now. The 60-name shape with 40 writes: 24334 -> 106.
One assignment, `{ }` and 8000 writes: 6633 -> 32.

Old and new script compared: every tracked .cts/.cjs/.ts/.js/.mjs file,
each line read for each identifier on it with no options and with the
Axis 2 options, plus findRawStateWrites and findUnstrippedContentWrites
per file (1715 files, 12.2M comparisons); 4.5M comparisons over 150000
fuzzed lines; 2.4M fuzzed binding lines; 150000 fuzzed files (44512
with findings). 0 differences. Mutants of the assignment regex, the loop regex
and the shared verdict key each show differences in the same harness.

New rows: lines read are bounded on a 200-write file (the row fails
without the cache); lookups are bounded on a 50-write branching file
(19950 lookups before, 1379 now, bound 1880); five whitespace shapes
keep their verdicts (time is not asserted); a null or undefined `stats`
changes no finding. The work-bound comment states the rule, not a
review.

Not bounded: a line holding many writes is read once per write, and a
call left open takes the rest of the file as its target. 8000 writes on
one 200 KB line: 2209 -> 627 ms; 8000 open calls on one line: 6341 ->
5292 ms.

commits.messageBody:
…nator after a whitespace run stays linear

The assignment tail `\s*=\s*([^=].*)$` kept the quadratic shape the
prefix had: `.` does not match `\r`, U+2028 or U+2029, so when one
follows a long whitespace run after `=`, each shorter run is tried and
rescanned up to it. `const p =<40000 spaces>x;\r` cost 1613 ms per read
on the previous head (32255 ms with 20 writes), and 531 ms per file
after the per-file cache. origin/next's Axis 3 reads through the same
tail (2268 ms for one such line there).

- assignmentHeadRegex matches up to the `=` and its whole whitespace
  run (a lookahead and backreference, as no possessive quantifier
  exists). assignedValue then decides the old tail from that one
  position: the capture could only start at the end of the run, or one
  character before it when that end is `=` or the end of the line, and
  `.*$` holds only when no line terminator follows. A failed head
  resumes one character on. The result is unchanged.
- findRawStateWrites reports `assignmentMatches`, the heads decided.

Probe, before (472cfb257) -> after (ms): `\r` ending, N = 1 and 20
writes: 1613, 32255 -> 1, 1; U+2028 ending: 1822, 36356 -> 1, 1.

Old and new script compared again, with `\r`, U+2028, U+2029 and
`=` runs added to the fuzz alphabet: 1715 files (12.2M comparisons),
4.5M comparisons over 150000 fuzzed lines, 150000 fuzzed files, 2.4M
fuzzed binding lines: 0 differences. Four mutants (a stricter keyword
form, a greedy loop pattern, the shared verdict key without its
boundary flag, and an off-by-one in the tail decision) show 7156,
38836, 23 and 186 differences.

Rows: a `\r` or U+2028 run decides at most one head per occurrence of
the name, with verdicts pinned; two writes across a `}` keep different
verdicts (pins the boundary flag in the shared key). Two test comments
that cited a review now state the rule.

The header now also discloses a line that repeats a declaration or
`for` header of the name many times as quadratic in that line (180 KB of
`const p: `: 4485 -> 1659 ms; 260 KB of `for (const p `: 3331 -> 3573
ms).

commits.messageBody:
…st the cap as unresolved

A call left open took the rest of the file as its first argument, once per
call, and each of many writes on one line re-read the line before it, so
both shapes cost time quadratic in the file or the line.

- MAX_RAW_WRITE_TEXT_LENGTH (4096, exported) bounds both reads. The longest
  first argument of a write over the 1715 tracked script and source files
  is 115 characters and the longest line before a call 129, so the cap is
  over 30 times either.
- A write past the cap is not resolved. It is reported as
  raw_state_write_unresolved on the raw-write axis, at most once per line,
  so the cap adds reports and never drops one.
- captureFirstArg takes an optional limit and reads at most limit + 1
  characters. The line before the call is measured before it is sliced.
- A finding's source is built once per line.
- The stats seam gains argumentChars and ownLineChars. New rows pin the cap
  at limit - 1, limit and limit + 1 for both reads, count the work for
  calls left open and for many writes on one line, and run the CLI on a
  call left open.
- The header now describes the cap and lists what it does not bound.

commits.messageBody:
…he writes past the budget as unresolved

Shapes of the resolver this change adds still cost time superlinear in a
file: many writes that each name a different variable, where each name's
first lookup read back to the enclosing named function (distinct names x
lines); a line that repeats a typed head, a for header or a destructuring
head, where each repeat scanned to the end of the line; many writes that
re-read one wide right-hand side; and writes that walk every earlier
assignment of their name past body boundaries.

- MAX_RAW_WRITE_RESOLVER_WORK (250000000, exported) bounds the work of
  resolving one file's writes. Over the 1728 tracked script and source
  files the most any file takes is 8186334 (tests/state.test.cjs, 1 MB),
  and in src/ 160872 (src/commands.cts), so the budget is over 30 times
  the first.
- Charged: each write's argument and line before the call, by length; each
  nearestPrecedingAssignment call, LOOKUP_WORK (64) plus the name; each line
  it reads, by lineReadWork: its length plus LINE_READ_WORK (32), times one
  more than its count of ':', '(', '[' and '{' when it holds the name,
  since each of those can start a scan to the end of the line; and each
  assignment right-hand side it resolves, by length.
- assignmentVerdict keeps an assignment's verdict below the write's line
  for later writes, under the same boundary flag as the other shared
  verdicts, so a wide right-hand side is read once. The assignment head
  regex is built once per name.
- A charge that would pass the budget is not made and its read is not
  done. The write that ran out and every later write in the file are
  reported as raw_state_write_unresolved, at most once per line.
- The budget is opt-in through the cache, so Axis 3's reads are unchanged.
- The stats seam gains resolverWork. New rows pin the budget at
  limit - 1, limit and limit + 1, count the work for distinct names, each
  repeated head, a shared right-hand side and boundary walks, and check
  that a write after the budget is spent is still reported.
- The header describes the budget in place of the shapes it left
  unbounded.

commits.messageBody:
…d the name in linear time

The resolver budget charged a line read by the line's length, but the
assignment head regex starts with the name, so where the name nearly
matches at every offset (a run of 'a' read for the name 'aaa...') one read
cost line length x name length. Two lines of 100000 'a's and 100 writes of
4000-character names took 22 s and spent a quarter of the budget.
String#includes has the same cost for a name with a repeated half.

- A line read under the budget finds the name's offsets with
  Knuth-Morris-Pratt (nameOccurrences), linear in the line, in place of
  includes. The head regex and the pattern-binding regex run sticky at
  those offsets only, which finds the same matches as the global scan.
- lineReadWork charges (line length + LINE_READ_WORK + occurrences x name
  length) x (1 + count of ':', '(', '[' and '{') when the name occurs, and
  line length + LINE_READ_WORK when it does not.
- Each name's regexes and failure table are built once (nameReader).
- Over the 1728 tracked script and source files the most any file now
  takes is 8267472 (tests/state.test.cjs) and in src/ 163185
  (src/commands.cts); MAX_RAW_WRITE_RESOLVER_WORK stays 250000000, 30.2
  and 1532 times those.
- A counted row pins the per-occurrence charge and the review's shape; the
  budget limit rows follow the new charge.
- Axis 3 does not pass a cache, so its reads are unchanged.
- The text cap's comment now cites the measurement after the rebase: over
  the 1728 tracked files the longest first argument and the longest line
  before a call are each 129 characters. The cap commit's message keeps
  the figures measured before the rebase, over 1715 files (115 and 129).
commits.messageHeadline: ci(#5104): charge a resolver read per occurrence of the name, and fin…

commits.messageBody:
…ved name, and search for names with indexOf

Each new name compiles its own regexes (about 70 us and 7 KB for a short
name, 350 us and 30 KB for a 256-character one), and that was not charged:
one distinct short name per write spent the budget in 44 s and 3.8 GB, and
4000-character distinct names ran out of heap inside findRawStateWrites,
which is a crash, not a reported write.

- Building a name's reader is charged READER_WORK (10000) plus
  READER_WORK_PER_CHAR (128) per character. The charge also bounds the
  memory the readers hold for the rest of the file.
- MAX_RESOLVED_NAME_LENGTH (256): a longer name is charged as the whole
  budget, so its write and every later write in the file are reported
  unresolved. Over the 1728 tracked script and source files the longest
  name the resolver looks up is 32 characters (27 in src/), and the longest
  identifier in src/ is 52.
- With names that short, the native indexOf search is cheap on the
  adversarial patterns probed (self-overlapping, near-miss, periodic and
  Fibonacci names up to 256 characters on 1 MB lines), so the
  Knuth-Morris-Pratt search is removed and indexOf is used again.
  The search for a name on a line stops once its occurrences could no
  longer be charged, so the read that runs out of budget does not first
  list every occurrence.
- The stats seam gains readersBuilt. New rows: one reader per distinct name,
  charged by length, for short and long names; and the name cap at
  limit - 1, limit and limit + 1. The text-cap row pads its name with
  spaces, so it no longer depends on the name cap.
- Over the 1728 tracked files the most any file now takes is 9315920
  (tests/state.test.cjs) and in src/ 308033 (src/commands.cts), so the
  budget of 250000000 is 26.8 and 812 times those. The most readers any
  file builds is 110 (18 in src/).

commits.messageBody:
identifiersIn dropped quoted strings with
/'(?:[^'\\]|\\.)*'|"(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*"/g, which, from every quote with no
closer, scans to the end of the text and fails, then tries the next quote.
A run of escaped quotes therefore cost time quadratic in its length, but was
charged by length. A template literal of escaped quotes reaches it as one
argument (the argument capture treats a backtick as a string; this regex
does not). Nested writes sharing one such literal took 26.6 s for a 999 KB
file, and one 400 KB right-hand side took 37.8 s.

- stripQuotedStrings gives the same result in one pass. A quote with no
  closer records where its failed scan stopped, and quotes of the same kind
  before that point are not tried: the failed scan passed each of them as
  the escaped half of a backslash pair, so a scan from one stops at the
  same point. A backslash before a line terminator also stops a scan, as
  `.` does not match one.
- Same output as the regex on 2500000 fuzzed strings (quotes of both
  kinds, backslash runs, \n, \r, U+2028, U+2029, backticks) and on every
  line and whole file of the 1728 tracked files.
- The backtick handling is unchanged in both places.
- The stats seam gains stringScanChars. A counted row puts a run of 1000
  escaped quotes in a target and in a right-hand side; each character is
  examined at most three times.
commits.messageHeadline: ci(#5104): strip quoted strings from a resolved expression in one pass
